parts.title: Booking a holiday cottage
parts.context: A man phones an agency to book a cottage for a family holiday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning a holiday cottage agency to book a cottage for a week in July. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Good morning, Heron Holiday Lets, Helen speaking.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Oh, hello. I'm calling about one of your cottages. We'd like to book a week in July, please. It's for our twentieth wedding anniversary.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Congratulations! Right, I'll just open up the booking form, then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man wants to book a cottage for a wedding anniversary, so 'wedding anniversary' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Can I take your name, please?

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Yes, it's Stuart Ackroyd.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Of course. It's A-C-K-R-O-Y-D.
script.tts: Of course. It's A, C, K, R, O, Y, D.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Thank you, Mr Ackroyd. And which dates were you hoping for?

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: We'd like to arrive on Saturday the twelfth of July and stay for a week.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Ah, now, our changeover day is always Friday, I'm afraid, so I can't offer you the twelfth. I could give you the eleventh, which is a Friday, or the eighteenth.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: The eighteenth would be too late for us, because my wife has to be back at work. So the eleventh it is, then. That's even better, really, because we'll get an extra night.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And how many of you will there be?

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Four adults, that's me and my wife, and my brother and his wife, and our two children. They're six and nine.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: So six people altogether. Let me see. Curlew Cottage only sleeps four, so that's too small, and Sandpiper Cottage is lovely, but it's about two miles from the sea. If you'd like to be near the beach, I'd suggest Kingfisher Cottage. It sleeps six, and it's right by the coast path.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Kingfisher sounds just right. Please put us down for that one.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Lovely. Is there anything else I should make a note of?

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Yes, we'd like to bring our dog. Is that allowed?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Dogs are welcome at Kingfisher, but there's a small charge to cover the extra cleaning. It's fifteen pounds a week for one dog.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: That's fine.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Could you tell me a bit about the garden? My wife loves eating outside in the evenings.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, it's completely fenced, so the dog will be quite safe. There's a patio with a table and chairs, and a barbecue, which is just the thing on a summer evening.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Wonderful. And how far is it to the beach?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The brochure says five minutes' walk, but I think that's only if you're in a hurry. With young children, I'd say it's more like ten.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Ten is fine. That's no distance at all. What about shopping? Is there a shop nearby, or will we have to drive to a supermarket?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: There's a village shop about half a mile away, which sells most of the basics. It's open until six on weekdays, but on Sundays it closes at four, so don't leave it too late.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: OK, I'll remember that. Now, can you tell me how much the cottage will cost for the week?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: For that week in July, the normal price is 680 pounds. But because you're booking early, we can give you a discount, so for you it will be 620 pounds in total.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: That sounds very reasonable.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, and one more thing. Bed linen and a welcome pack are included, but we don't supply towels, so you'll need to bring your own.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Thanks for telling me. I'd have forgotten!

script.speaker: helen
script.text: I'll email the confirmation and a map to you this afternoon.

script.speaker: stuart
script.text: Brilliant. Thanks very much for your help.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Thank you for calling, Mr Ackroyd.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A new exhibition on the history of glass
parts.context: A museum guide introduces an exhibition to a group of visitors.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a museum guide introducing a new exhibition about the history of glass. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashgrove Museum. My name's Hannah, and I'm going to introduce our new exhibition, Fire and Sand: Five Thousand Years of Glass. It opened last Saturday, and it runs until the end of March.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: People often ask me why we chose glass. You might think it's because of the anniversary of the old Bellfield glassworks, but that isn't until next year. And although we're always pleased to see more families, that wasn't the reason either. The real reason is that last spring the museum was left a collection of nearly four hundred pieces by a local collector, Edith Marlowe, who asked in her will for it to be shown to the public.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Now, let's start at the beginning. You may know the story that glass was discovered by accident, when some sailors lit a fire on a beach and the sand melted. It's a lovely story, but there's no evidence for it at all. What archaeologists have actually found are tiny beads and small bottles from Egypt and Mesopotamia, and they seem to have been made as jewellery and decoration for wealthy families.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: The next big change was glassblowing, about two thousand years ago. Before that, a single small bottle could take a whole day to make. With blowing, it took minutes, so glass stopped being a luxury and became cheap enough for ordinary Roman households. What it didn't do, though, was improve windows. Roman window glass stayed thick and cloudy, and really clear sheets didn't come until very much later.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: In the Middle Ages, the centre of glassmaking moved to Venice. In 1291, all of the city's glassmakers were ordered to move to the island of Murano. People often say this was to stop them passing their secrets to rival cities, and that did become a reason later on. But the original order was about safety. The furnaces burned day and night, and most of Venice was built of wood, so the authorities were afraid of a fire.
script.tts: In the Middle Ages, the centre of glassmaking moved to Venice. In twelve ninety-one, all of the city's glassmakers were ordered to move to the island of Murano. People often say this was to stop them passing their secrets to rival cities, and that did become a reason later on. But the original order was about safety. The furnaces burned day and night, and most of Venice was built of wood, so the authorities were afraid of a fire.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: So, what can you actually do here? We spent a lot of money on a virtual-reality furnace, which lets you step inside a glassworks, and we assumed it would be the star attraction. There's also a short film in the first gallery, which most people walk straight past. In fact, visitors have spent the longest at the touch table, where you can handle everything from a Roman bottle to a modern phone screen, so I'd head there first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Right, shall we go in? There are four galleries, and I'll just point out one thing to look for in each.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Gallery One, Beginnings, covers the ancient world. The oldest object in the whole exhibition is here, a small blue vessel about three thousand four hundred years old. The old label calls it a bottle, but it has a handle, so it's clearly a jug.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Gallery Two, Colour and Light, is about medieval stained glass. Most people expect windows to come from churches or cathedrals, but our finest piece was rescued from a ruined abbey on the north coast.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Gallery Three, Glass and Discovery, is about science. Beside the lenses and early telescopes, you'll see a copy of the glass prism that Isaac Newton used in the 1660s to show that sunlight is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.
script.tts: Gallery Three, Glass and Discovery, is about science. Beside the lenses and early telescopes, you'll see a copy of the glass prism that Isaac Newton used in the sixteen sixties to show that sunlight is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: And Gallery Four is Glass Today. The centrepiece is a chandelier by the artist Tomas Reyes, made from recycled bottles. He planned to use four hundred, but the first design looked too small, so it ended up with 600. On Saturdays, you can also join a workshop in this gallery and make your own glass paperweight to take home.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: That's all from me. Does anyone have any questions before we go in?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A case study of a family bakery
parts.context: Two business students discuss their case study with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Nadia and Oscar, talking to their tutor, Dr Hughes, about a case study of a family-owned bakery. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Come in, both of you. I've read your draft case study of Brindle's Bakery. Before I give you my comments, remind me why you chose that business.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Well, I used to buy my lunch there, but I'd never met the family. And their accounts aren't published, so that made life harder, if anything. What really drew us in was that they're facing a big decision this year about whether to expand, and we wanted to see how a family firm actually makes a choice like that.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Good. And how did you collect your information?

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Mostly through interviews. We were worried the family would be too busy, but Joanne Brindle gave us a whole afternoon, and the staff were surprisingly frank. The hard part was the money. They would only tell us the total sales. The profit figures for each shop were off limits.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Now, my comments. The literature review is thorough, and I don't mind the length. And your findings are very clearly presented. My concern is the analysis. You explain the three-circle model of family firms very well, but then you never use it. You don't say where Walter Brindle, or his daughter, would fit in the model.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: We thought the explanation would be enough.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: It isn't, I'm afraid. Theory has to be applied to the case, otherwise it's just decoration. Now, one other thing. You've quoted several members of staff by name. Those quotations are the best thing in your draft, so I'd keep them, but I'd take the names out.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: We could ask each of them to sign a permission form, couldn't we?

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: You could, but that takes time, and some of them might say no. It's much simpler to leave the names out.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: OK. Should we also interview another family bakery, so that we can compare?

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: It would be nice, but you've only got two weeks, and the introduction is fine as it is. I'd spend the time making sure your facts about Brindle's are right. Send the family a summary of your findings before you submit.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Good idea. We'll email Joanne tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Right, now your stakeholder section. You describe five people with different views about the future of the business. Take me through them.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Yes. Walter Brindle is the founder. He's eighty-one, but he still comes in at five every morning. He's happy for the business to grow, he says, as long as nobody touches the recipes.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: His daughter Joanne is the managing director. A regional supermarket chain has offered her a contract, and she's convinced that's the best way to grow.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Then there's her brother Martin, the head baker. He isn't interested in the consultant's idea of cutting the range. He'd like to bake more kinds of bread, not fewer. What he really loves is teaching. He already runs informal baking sessions on Sunday mornings for local people, and he'd like to make those a regular part of the business.

script.speaker: oscar
script.text: Joanne's daughter, Fiona, joined last year to run the marketing. She's the one who wants to sell bread online, with next-day delivery across the region.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: And finally there's Gareth, the finance manager. He isn't a member of the family, but his views carry a lot of weight. He isn't against any of these ideas, but he's very nervous about borrowing money. The bakery opened a shop in Eastbridge in 2015, took out a big loan, and had to close it within a year.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: That's a clear summary. Make sure your recommendations follow from those positions.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: We will. Thank you, Dr Hughes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how desert animals survive the heat
parts.context: A lecture about the ways in which animals cope with extreme heat in deserts.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how animals survive in hot deserts. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to look at how animals survive in one of the harshest environments on Earth, the hot desert. In the Sahara, the surface of the sand can reach seventy degrees Celsius, and in some years there's no rain at all. So desert animals face two linked problems: how to avoid overheating, and how to avoid running out of water. Most of my examples come from the Sahara, but the same principles apply in deserts all over the world. I'm going to look at their solutions under three headings: behaviour, body structure and physiology.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: First, behaviour. The simplest strategy is to keep out of the heat. Just a few centimetres below the surface, the sand is far cooler and more stable, so many small mammals spend the day in underground burrows and only come out after dark. The jerboa, a tiny hopping rodent, is a good example. Animals that have to be active in daylight make use of shade, and the Cape ground squirrel has an unusual way of creating its own. It raises its bushy tail over its back, like a parasol, and sits in the shadow.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Second, body structure. Here, the fennec fox is a classic example. It's the smallest fox in the world, but its ears are enormous, and they're full of blood vessels very close to the skin. As the blood flows through them, the heat escapes into the air. The ears also help the fox to hear insects moving underground, but cooling is their main job. The jackrabbit of North America has the same feature.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Even insects have clever solutions. The silver ant, which lives in the Sahara, goes out at midday, when the sand is at its hottest, because that's when the lizards that hunt it have retreated underground. It's covered in tiny silver hairs, which have a triangular shape and reflect the sunlight, so the ant stays much cooler than you'd expect. It also has very long legs, which lift its body well clear of the burning sand. Even so, it can only stay out for a few minutes at a time.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Third, physiology, and here the key issue is water. The kangaroo rat of North America almost never drinks. It gets the moisture it needs from the dry seeds that it eats, not from green plants, because water is released inside its body as the food is broken down. It also loses very little. Its urine is extremely concentrated, and its nose recovers moisture from the air that it breathes out. In fact, it can live its whole life without taking a single drink.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then there's the camel, which is surrounded by myths. Many people believe that its hump stores water. It doesn't. The hump is a store of fat, which the camel can use as an energy reserve when food is scarce. What camels do have is a remarkable tolerance of dehydration. They let their body temperature rise by several degrees during the day, rather than sweating to keep it down. And a camel can lose up to a quarter of its body weight in water and survive, whereas a human is in serious trouble after losing about ten per cent. And when it finds water, a thirsty camel can drink well over a hundred litres in around ten minutes.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Some animals even collect water from the air. The thorny devil, a small spiny lizard from Australia, has tiny grooves between the scales on its skin. When dew forms on its body overnight, or when it stands on damp sand, the water is drawn along those grooves until it reaches the corner of the lizard's mouth. In effect, the whole body works like a drinking straw.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, birds. Birds have no sweat glands, so they can't sweat, and many desert species, such as nightjars, use a different technique, known as gular fluttering. They open their beaks and vibrate the skin of the throat very rapidly. Water evaporates from the moist surface and takes heat away with it, in much the same way that sweating cools us.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So, no single trick works on its own. Most desert animals combine several: they avoid the worst of the heat, they are built to lose it, and they treat every drop of water as precious. Next week, we'll look at how climate change is putting these strategies under pressure.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
